Hope and pressure mix in Resolution 1952, adopted by the General Assembly on 11 December 1963, on the question of Northern Rhodesia. The British-run land, soon to become Zambia, stood near the end of colonial rule. The Assembly had read the report of its decolonization team and heard the ruling power report fresh steps toward a new constitution that same month.

The text states again the fixed right of the people of Northern Rhodesia to rule themselves and stand free. It notes with pleasure that votes for a new law-making council will be held in January 1964. Britain is asked to fix, with the new elected rulers, a date for freedom, and as soon as can be. The hope is voiced that no new block will bar the way.

United action toward a world free of nuclear arms is urged in Resolution A/69/52, from the General Assembly's sixty-ninth session. All states, it holds, must take fresh, workable steps toward the total end of such arms. The end goal of all arms work is named: full disarmament under strict and sound world check.

Deep worry at the ruinous toll of any use of nuclear arms runs through the text. All states must keep to world law at all times, the law of war among it. Every effort must be made, it holds, to shun the use of such arms at all. The vote stands in a yearly chain that keeps the end goal in sight.

Raúl de la Fuente-Fernández weighed a hopeful idea about Alzheimer's disease in a 2006 paper: if doctors could protect nerve cells, neuroprotection, would fewer people develop the disease? Alzheimer's incidence, the rate of new cases, rises steeply with age, and no treatment then could prevent it. Prevention was the prize.

His analysis considers the impact neuroprotection could have on incidence, reasoning from what is known about how the disease develops over years before symptoms. Even delaying onset changes the arithmetic of an aging population, since many would die of other causes first. The paper makes that population-level case, a style of argument that now anchors Alzheimer's prevention planning.

Ambassador Averell Harriman wrote a secret memorandum at Cairo on 23 November 1943 recording a talk with Soviet official Andrey Vyshinsky. While waiting to see the President, Harriman had sounded him out, at Harry Hopkins' request, on Soviet views of several Mediterranean problems.

On Lebanon, Harriman said bluntly that America could not let the French Committee wreck world trust in its pledges of freedom, and Vyshinsky answered that his government could hold no other view. On Italy's king, Vyshinsky kept an open mind but leaned against keeping him, saying any institution blocking the Moscow principles must move aside. Both men agreed that Yugoslav leader Mihailović had been not merely useless in the war, but harmful.

Steve Early, the President's secretary, sent Harry Hopkins a longer telegram from Washington on 2 December 1943, supplementing his earlier report of that day on the Cairo communiqué's reception. It returns to the Reuters leak that had scooped the official release.

Early reports bitter resentment among American newspapers. He reports formal protests to Minister Bracken and to Ambassador Halifax. He reports a heated debate in the House of Commons that day, where Bracken disclaimed responsibility. The Reuters story had gone out generally some thirty-three hours early, though British censors kept it out of English papers. It gave away nearly the entire Cairo story except the communiqué's text. Washington reporters, Early says, blame the British, not the Americans, and kept their own correspondents' fuller accounts unpublished until the release hour.

The finding serves environmental engineering. Bioelectrochemistry turns waste into negative emissions. Chao Li turned waste into negative emissions. Circular economy needs bioelectrochemical systems.
pmc-13463152: Impact of obstructive sleep apnea on arrhythmic risk was studied in ischemic heart disease and hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. The apnea-arrhythmia link was quantified. The finding guides cardiology. Sleep apnea raises arrhythmia risk. Qingqing Li quantified apnea-arrhythmia risk. Sudden death prevention needs sleep assessment.
pmc-13423152: Parent-delivered hand-arm bimanual intensive training including lower extremity was tested for young children with bilateral cerebral palsy. The home therapy was evaluated. The finding guides pediatrics. Parents can deliver intensive CP therapy. Nguyen tested parent-delivered CP therapy. Bilateral CP needs home-based intensity.
pmc-13559652: Global research trends in fecal microbiota transplantation combined with immune checkpoint inhibitors were mapped for cancer. The FMT-immunotherapy field was surveyed. The finding guides oncology. Gut transplants may boost checkpoint therapy. Yingying Hu mapped FMT-immunotherapy trends. Combination immunotherapy needs microbiome evidence.
arxiv-2606-04452: DeltaDiff: training-free, physics-guided machine learning was developed for predicting mutant protein structures. The protein AI was built. The finding serves bioinformatics. Physics guidance predicts mutant structures. Yajie Cai predicted mutant structures physics-first. Rare disease needs structure prediction. Cai's DeltaDiff aids drug design.
arxiv-2606-04552: LDARNet: DNA adaptive representation network was built with learnable tokenization for genomic modeling. The genomic AI was engineered. The finding serves bioinformatics. Adaptive tokenization models DNA better. Daria Ledneva tokenized DNA adaptively. Precision medicine needs genomic tokenization. Ledneva's LDARNet improves variant calling.
arxiv-2606-04852: A note on the Kullback-Leibler divergence was written for discretized empirical distributions. The information theory note was derived. The finding serves statistics. Discretization affects KL divergence. Osaki analyzed discretized KL divergence. Model evaluation needs divergence care. Osaki's note refines information criteria.
arxiv-2606-05152: Reinforcement learning usually runs on thin feedback — a single score per action. This paper learns from rich feedback instead, keeping the full distribution of possible outcomes, and pairs it with a distributional version of DAgger, a classic imitation-learning algorithm. The combination lets agents learn faster from detailed human guidance rather than sparse rewards.
arxiv-2606-05552: An image tokenizer that compresses well usually generates poorly, and vice versa. This paper balances image compression and generation with bootstrapped tokenization — a tokenizer that improves itself by learning from its own outputs. One tokenizer good at both jobs simplifies the whole image-AI pipeline.
arxiv-2606-05652: Generating data with conditions — a molecule with this property, an image in that style — usually needs labeled examples. CoFi-UCGen does coarse-to-fine unsupervised conditional generation without label priors, discovering the conditioning structure on its own. Label-free control makes generative models useful where annotations are scarce.
arxiv-2606-05852: Speech and singing are usually modeled separately — but the human voice does both. UniVoice is a unified model for speech and singing voice generation, learning one vocal instrument instead of two. A single voice model sings the words and speaks the song.
arxiv-2606-06252: Language models reason in hidden latents — but nobody checks whether that reasoning is any good. This paper closes the loop via test-time reconstruction: forcing the model to reconstruct its inputs from its latents, exposing hollow reasoning. Reconstruction turns hidden thought into something verifiable.
arxiv-2606-06352: Grassmannians — spaces of all k-dimensional subspaces — are geometry's favorite testing grounds. This paper computes their equivariant quantum cohomology via the Clifford algebra: counting curves with symmetry through algebraic machinery. The Clifford route offers a fresh computational handle on quantum intersection theory.
arxiv-2606-06752: Code quality rots without constant care — but big refactors are risky. Pomona improves code continuously at Bloomberg via small, automated changes: tiny safe steps, compounded. The system proves relentless small fixes beat heroic rewrites. Compounding improvements win at scale.
arxiv-2606-06952: Semiconductors under modulated light reveal nonlinear dynamics in the frequency domain. This paper characterizes those dynamics using modulated photoexcitation. The characterization probes how materials respond to light. Frequency-domain analysis reveals hidden dynamics. Modulation unlocks the nonlinear response. The method is non-destructive and precise.
arxiv-2606-07152: Symbolic regression finds equations from data — but what if there is no data? This data-free approach solves equations with symbolic regression alone. The method discovers formulas from the equations themselves. Equations yield their secrets without data. Symbolic methods are powerful.
arxiv-2606-07252: Answering questions over multimodal documents needs selecting the right evidence. This paper uses constrained dominant sets for that selection. The constraints keep the evidence coherent. Evidence selection needs coherence across modalities. The constraints enforce sensible document understanding. The method is principled.
arxiv-2606-00052: Factories making multiple products need process monitoring that knows which product is running. These product-aware deep autoencoders monitor multi-product cyber-physical systems robustly. The awareness prevents false alarms. False alarms cost modern factories real money. Product awareness prevents expensive operational mistakes.
arxiv-2606-07452: SS 433's western jet — from a microquasar in W50 — shines in hard X-rays. This paper studies its emission, spectral evolution, and comparison to the eastern jet. The jets are nature's particle accelerators. Microquasars act as stellar-scale particle accelerators. Hard X-rays reveal their jet physics.
arxiv-2606-07552: Multi-agent LLM systems with symbolic reasoning develop memory-mediated ecosystem dynamics. This paper triggers and studies them. The ecosystems reveal emergent collective behavior.  Collective machine behavior consistently surprises even experienced designers. Memory-mediated interactions create genuinely novel multi-agent ecosystems worth studying carefully.
tob-0152:
Crowley's Vision and the Voice records his workings of 1909 in Algeria, where he scryed the thirty Aethyrs of the Enochian system. Vision by vision, angels, abysses, and terrible splendors pass before him. The notebooks became one of Thelema's central records of attainment.

Volume four of the notebook edition continues the transcribed series. Crowley crosses the Abyss in the visions and claims the grade of Magister Templi, master of the temple. The text is dense, symbolic, and meant for initiates. The material remains under copyright, with no public-domain text distributed here. Students of Crowley treat the work as his spiritual diary at its most intense.
tob-13152:
A. E. Waite devoted his late work The Holy Grail to the legends of the Grail, the vessel of the Last Supper and the Crucifixion. Waite was both occultist and scholar of Christian mysticism. He had chased the Grail's meaning through years of study.

He traces the tales from early romances onward, asks how they took Christian shape, and argues the Grail hides a secret tradition of the church. The book is dense, learned, and fully Waite's own in its claims. Readers of Arthurian romance and of occult history alike treat it as the mature sum of his Grail research.
maidstone-six-witches-1652:
Six women were condemned at the Maidstone assizes in 1652, and their story was sold as A Prodigious and Tragicall History. The Kent trial ranks among the major witch cases of the Interregnum, the years when England had no king. The pamphlet gives the charges and the court's sentences.

Its title sells wonder and sorrow at once, and the text inside keeps that tone. Readers learn who the six were, what harm was laid to them, and how the court dealt with each. The case shows the witch trial alive and well under the republic. Print and panic still walked hand in hand in 1652.
wapping-witch-relation-1652:
London itself had a witch case in 1652, told in The Witch of Wapping. The pamphlet gives the full relation of the charge and trial in the riverside parish of Wapping. A city case drew eyes that county trials could not.

The text walks readers through the claims, the court work, and the fate of the accused. It brings the hunt for witches to the crowded streets and docks of the capital. Country fears look strange in town dress, and the print knows it. The case shows the panic could touch even the heart of London.
wapping-witch-answer-1652:
Rival prints of the Wapping witch case drew a sharp reply in 1652. A Declaration in Answer to Pamphlets concerning the Witch of Wapping takes the other accounts apart point by point. Such print fights were common, but few over witch cases survive so fully.

The writer charges the first pamphlets with false reports and works to set the record straight. Readers watch two camps argue over what was said, done, and proved. The quarrel shows the witch panic fought out in the press as much as in court. It is a rare, clear look at how trial news was made and unmade.
chadwell-memo-1952:
A CIA science chief urged Washington to take the flying saucers in earnest in September 1952. Marshall Chadwell's memo to the Director of Central Intelligence asks the National Security Council to act. Chadwell ran the Office of Scientific Intelligence in a summer of mass sightings.

He warns that the saucer reports touch air defense and public calm at once. His ask set in train the Robertson Panel, which met the next winter in secret. That panel taught the agency to calm and debunk the reports in public. The memo is the paper that made UFOs a Washington question.
buckley-life-and-adventures-1852:
William Buckley lived wild for thirty-two years, and his Life and Adventures, out in 1852, tells how. Buckley was a felon sent to the far south land who fled to the bush in 1803. The Wathaurong folk took him in. He dwelt as one of them till new white men came in 1835 and he stepped out of a lost age, a giant in skins.

John Morgan shaped his tale for print. Midst wars, hunts, and rites stands talk of the bunyip, the dread beast of the swamps. The book is a rare guest's tale. It grips throughout.
voltaire-micromegas-1752:
Voltaire wrote Micromegas in 1752 as a tale with a sharp point. A giant from a star of Sirius, eight leagues tall, roams the sky. He picks up a small friend from Saturn on his way. The pair come to Earth and at first miss the folk who live here.

With a lens of cut gems they spot a ship full of men of thought. Talk with the small crew shows both pride and true wit in men. The giant laughs at wars fought for specks of mud. The tale is a root work of tales of guests from the stars.
rosicrucian-manifestos-vaughan-1652:
Thomas Vaughan put the Fama and Confessio into English in 1652, the first English Rosicrucian texts. The two manifestos first came out in German lands in 1614 and 1615. They claimed a hidden brotherhood held deep lore and sought to reform the world.

The Fama tells of Christian Rosenkreuz, his travels, and his vault tomb. The Confessio calls scholars to join the work and share their finds. No proof of the brotherhood ever surfaced, yet the call stirred Europe. Vaughan's version spread the Rosy Cross myth across England in time. Alchemists and seekers mined these pages for secret lore.
hawthorne-blithedale-romance-1852:
Nathaniel Hawthorne published The Blithedale Romance in 1852, his novel of a utopian farm community. The book is a roman à clef of Brook Farm, where Hawthorne had lived in 1841. It is the first great American novel of utopian community and its discontents in fiction.

Poet Miles Coverdale, the narrator, spies on his fellow reformers from trees and hermitage hides in Blithedale. Hollingsworth, a stern prison reformer, bends the commune to his single driving cause of reforming criminals. Zenobia, proud and passionate, and meek Priscilla fall into a triangle that ends in river death. Coverdale's voyeur gaze makes him the least trusted teller Hawthorne ever built into a tale here. The book asks if reformers love mankind or only their own grand schemes.
turgenev-sportsmans-sketches-1852:
Ivan Turgenev published A Sportsman's Sketches in 1852, his twenty-five sketches of peasant life under serfdom. The sketches exposed serfdom's cruelty so tellingly that the book is credited with helping free the serfs. Turgenev, hunting with his spaniel, listens more than he shoots, and Russia heard its peasants speak.

Khor and Kalinych, the first sketch, pairs a shrewd, practical serf with a dreamy, gentle one in Orel province. Bezhin Meadow gives peasant boys telling ghost tales by a night fire, in pages of famous beauty and dread. Landowners, overseers, and serf actors and singers fill out a survey no statistics could match for truth of life. The sportsman's mild voice let radical matter past the censor into the conscience of the reading class of Russia. Alexander II kept the book by him, it was said, when he signed emancipation.
newman-idea-of-university-1852:
When Newman became rector of a new Catholic university in Dublin, he gave the lectures published in 1852 as The Idea of a University. They define what a university is for, beyond training for jobs or trades. The book became a foundational text of Christian higher education.

Newman argues that knowledge is its own end, and that a liberal education trains the mind to think clearly and whole. He also defends a seat for theology among the sciences, since each field of study needs the others to stay honest. College teachers still quote his lectures in fights over what schools owe their students.
ashmole-theatrum-chemicum-britannicum-16:
Elias Ashmole, the antiquary whose museum still bears his name at Oxford, edited the Theatrum Chemicum Britannicum in 1652. The anthology gathers English alchemical verse from the Middle Ages and the Tudor age. Ashmole meant to prove that England had its own noble line of adepts.

The poems of Thomas Norton, George Ripley, and the writers who used the name Lully fill its pages in their old spelling. Ashmole adds notes, lives of the authors, and a defense of the art against its mockers. The book preserved the canon of English alchemy that later scholars still study from his pages.
culpeper-english-physician-1652:
Nicholas Culpeper was a London herbalist who broke the physicians' monopoly by translating their Latin pharmacopoeia into English. His English Physician, published in 1652, is his herbal, the guide that put physic in every English household. Culpeper assigns each plant its ruling planet and its virtues together.

He describes hundreds of English herbs, where they grow, when to gather them, and what ills they cure, in plain words for poor readers. His astrological frame tells the user which herb fights which disease by the stars' sympathy and opposition. No medical book of the age reached more homes, or stayed in print so long.
gulistan-eastwick-1852:
Edward B. Eastwick published his English Gulistan in 1852, the first translation of Saadi's Rose Garden into prose and verse together. Saadi of Shiraz wrote the Gulistan in Persian in 1258, after a lifetime of travel and study. Eastwick adds a life of the author drawn from the Atish Kadah.

Kings, dervishes, schoolboys, and wrestlers pass through eight chapters of tales and maxims. Each short story lands on a line of counsel about mercy, contentment, speech, or power. Saadi mixes prose with verse morals in the Persian manner, and Eastwick follows him. Persians have quoted the Gulistan for seven centuries as their handbook of wisdom. Eastwick's pioneering version opened it to the English world.
florus-epitome-roman-history-watson-1852:
Lucius Annaeus Florus cast the whole history of Rome as the life of one man, from youth to age, in his Epitome of about 120 CE. John Selby Watson's English version came out in 1852, with a notice on Florus. The short work runs from Romulus to Augustus.

Rome grows through childhood wars in Italy, storms to manhood in the Punic and eastern wars, then turns its strength on itself in civil strife. Florus writes with heat and color, more poet than clerk. His book was read all through the Middle Ages. It gives the quickest bold sketch of Rome's rise that Latin kept.
ovid-heroides-amores-art-riley-1852:
Henry T. Riley turned Ovid's early love poems into English prose for Bohn's library in 1852. The volume gathers four works of the young Ovid: the Heroides, the Amores, the Art of Love, and the Remedy of Love. Together they made Ovid the teacher of love for the Roman world and for ages after.

The Heroides are letters from mythic heroines, Penelope, Dido, and Medea among them, to the men who left them. The Amores chase a mistress through Rome in witty elegies. The Art of Love then gives mock-serious rules for winning and keeping a lover, and the Remedy cures the wound. Riley's prose keeps the sense plain for students.
braid-magic-witchcraft-animal-magnetism-:
Braid's mature statement came in Magic, Witchcraft, Animal Magnetism, Hypnotism, and Electro-Biology, in its enlarged third edition of 1852. Witch trials, demonic possession, and mesmeric marvels crowd its pages. Braid rereads them all as misunderstood nervous and mental phenomena. What ages blamed on demons, he assigns to trance, suggestion, and disease.

The book gathers his whole demystification project between two covers. History supplies his cases, and his physiology supplies the keys. Electro-biology, a stage name for hypnotic shows, gets its share of analysis. The work caps a decade in which he remade the field. It shows a surgeon arguing with centuries of fear. The argument stays humane throughout.
zoist-vol-10-1852:
The Zoist's tenth volume runs from April 1852 to January 1853. A decade of Elliotson's journal now stands in print. Mesmeric practice reports arrive from a loyal band of doctors and amateurs. Trance surgery, once the headline, now shares space with subtler mental cases.

Cerebral physiology still names half the journal's mission on its cover. Somnambulists and their feats draw the curious, as ever. The movement's complete record would fill thirteen volumes by 1856. Volume ten shows a cause grown older, its hopes and habits fixed. What the medical world dismissed, these pages preserved. That preservation is the set's lasting service.
hahnemann-lesser-writings-1852:
Samuel Hahnemann wrote far more than the Organon, and The Lesser Writings of 1852 gathers that scattered work in one place. R. E. Dudgeon edited the volume, with notes by Richard Hughes. Essays, letters, and case notes sit side by side, spanning Hahnemann's long career as the founder of homeopathy and its first arguer.

Some pieces argue with critics, while others record single cures or early drug trials. Together they show his ideas forming well before the famous system took shape. Students who know only the Organon find a fuller Hahnemann here: sharper, more restless, and always testing his rules against practice.
plos-pone-0003452:
Marina Cardó-Vila and co-authors pulled a drug clue from a cancer patient in this 2008 paper. They screened fragments selected in that patient for useful binders. One peptide matched part of human interleukin-11, a signaling protein. Interleukin-11 is already approved to treat low platelet counts after chemotherapy.

The peptide mapped to domain I of the protein. That spot is where the protein meets its receptor. A binder for that site could tune the signal up or down. The work gives drug designers a foothold on a cancer-related pathway. Screens drawn from patients can surface binders that pure lab design might miss.
plos-pone-0003552:
Meredith E. Young, Geoffrey R. Norman, and Karin R. Humphreys studied media effects on disease fear in this 2008 paper. Global talk of pandemics has raised reporting on outbreaks. Heavy coverage may shift how risky diseases seem to the public. Their studies tested that influence directly.

High levels of press reporting changed perceptions of disease. Readers judged covered diseases as more threatening than facts warranted. The popular press thus sets the public sense of danger. Health officials must plan messages with that power in mind. Outbreak scares show this effect at its strongest in daily news cycles.
plos-pone-0003652:
Reuben Saba, Chelsey D. Goodman, Rhiannon L. C. H. Huzarewich, and colleagues published this brain study in PLOS ONE in 2008. MicroRNAs are tiny RNA pieces that tune how genes are used in cells. Little was known about their part in diseases where brain tissue breaks down.

The team profiled microRNAs in prion disease, where misfolded proteins damage the brain. A set pattern of changes appeared as the disease advanced, forming a signature of the damage. Such a signature could help track the disease and point to steps where failing neurons might be helped.
plos-pone-0003752:
Francisco Caiado, Carla Real, Tânia Carvalho, and colleagues published this vascular study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Cells from bone marrow can become vascular precursor cells that help build new blood vessels. They take part in normal vessel growth, cancer growth, low blood flow repair, and wound healing.

The team adjusted Notch signaling in these precursor cells. Tuning that pathway changed the cells' power to grow vessels and support healing. The dial offers a way to control the body's own repair crew, for better vessel growth where tissue needs it.
plos-pone-0003852:
Antje Fischer-Rosinsky, Eva Fisher, Peter Kovacs, and colleagues published this meta-analysis in PLOS ONE in 2008. SOCS3 links cytokine signals to insulin resistance, making it a candidate gene for type 2 diabetes. A common variant, A+930 to G, had been picked from HapMap data as the tag to test.

The authors pooled four independent study populations to test that variant. They found no association between the SOCS3 tagging variant and type 2 diabetes. The clear negative result closes the case on one suspect and lets diabetes genetics focus its search elsewhere.
plos-pone-0003952:
Sara K. Lindén, Timothy H. J. Florin, and Michael A. McGuckin reviewed mucus changes during gut infection in 2008. Bacterial gut infections sicken and kill people around the world. A mouse infection with Citrobacter rodentium models two human E. coli diseases. Mucus glycoproteins form the gut's first protective layer.

Their PLOS ONE article follows how that mucus layer changes during infection. The mucins shift in amount and type as bacteria attack. Those shifts can help or hinder the germs that live there. Knowing the pattern clarifies how the gut defends its lining. It appeared in PLOS ONE, and the full text is free for any reader to check.
plos-pone-0004052:
Jeffrey W. Habig, P. Joseph Aruscavage, and Brenda L. Bass studied gene silencing in worms in 2008. RNA interference starts when Dicer cuts double-stranded RNA into small pieces. In C. elegans, Dicer needs a helper protein called RDE-4. Without it, RNA interference normally fails at step one.

Their PLOS ONE article reports high RNA doses bypass that need. With enough trigger RNA, silencing worked even without RDE-4. The exception reveals a backup route into the silencing machinery. Dose effects like this matter for labs designing RNA experiments. It was printed in PLOS ONE, where the full text stays free to read.
plos-pone-0004152:
Anirban Chakraborty and colleagues published this developmental study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Ribosomes are the cell's protein factories, and their building blocks, ribosomal proteins, do more than hold the factory together. One of them, L11, was recently shown to control the tumour suppressor p53 by binding its regulator MDM2.

Using zebrafish embryos, the team asked what happens to development when L11 is lost. They report that losing L11 disrupts embryonic development through a cell-death response that depends on p53. The finding links a ribosome part to the guard system that decides whether damaged cells live or die.
plos-pone-0004252:
Andrew Farke, Ewan Wolff, and Darren Tanke published this dinosaur study in PLOS ONE in 2009. The horns and frill of Triceratops have been read two ways: as display structures or as weapons used against rivals and predators. Lesions in the bone, including reactive bone growth, healing fractures, and possible punctures, offer a way to test the weapon idea.

The authors gathered evidence of such injuries on Triceratops skulls. They present it as evidence of combat between these dinosaurs. If the marks match fighting, the great frill was not just a billboard but a shield in real fights.
plos-pone-0004352:
John Hagan and colleagues published this imprinting study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Genomic imprinting is an exception to Mendelian genetics: imprinted genes are expressed from only one parent's copy, depending on parental origin. In mammals these genes are critical in development and physiology, and faulty imprinting is tied to disease.

The team defined the imprinted Dlk1-Dio3 cluster on mouse chromosome 12qF1. They report that at least ten genes define the cluster. The cluster sits on mouse chromosome 12, in the band called qF1. A full census of the region is the groundwork for understanding the disorders tied to it.
plos-pone-0004452: In 2009, Tavabi, Elling, and Dobel watched live brains hear speech shortcuts. Place-of-articulation changes in casual speech shifted auditory neural activity. The MEG scans caught the brain adapting live. The finding maps human speech perception. The sound shortcuts are universal in speech.
plos-pone-0004552: In 2009, Koch, Ledermann, and Urwyler dissected a fly protein's control switch. Systematic functional analysis of Bicaudal-D serine phosphorylation was done. The phosphorylation sites tuned the protein finely. The finding maps posttranslational control tricks. The genetic screen used fruit flies.
plos-pone-0004652: In 2009, a team found a signal steering white cells anew today. The signal via Vav proteins tuned white-cell tissue travel well. The signal guided the cells quite precisely. The neat finding maps germ-fighting tactics. The cell call-up is rapid.
plos-pone-0004752: In 2009, Kulkarni, Dhakal, and Slechta probed bacterial syringes in urinary infections anew here. Type II secretion and type IV pili in UPEC were tested. The syringes proved needless indeed. The study maps bacterial harm pathways. The key traits are virulence factors.
douglass-fourth-of-july-1852:
Frederick Douglass spoke in Corinthian Hall at Rochester, New York, on Monday, July 5, 1852. The speech was printed as a pamphlet the same year. He opens by confessing nerves and doubt about his powers before so large a crowd.

Then he turns to the hard question in his title: what the Fourth of July means to the slave. For those still in chains, he argues, the day mocks them with talk of freedom they cannot share. Born enslaved himself, Douglass answers with fierce and exact logic. The address still stands among the greatest speeches in American history.
stowe-uncle-toms-cabin-1852:
Harriet Beecher Stowe published Uncle Tom's Cabin in 1852, with the subtitle Life Among the Lowly. The contents alone map a wide cast, from an evening in Tom's cabin to a Quaker settlement. Early chapters show Eliza learning she may lose her child and choosing flight.

Eliza's escape across the ice, little Eva, Topsy, and the cruel Simon Legree became known to millions. Tom's faith under harsh masters forms the moral core of the long tale. The novel sold hundreds of thousands of copies in its first year. It turned broad feeling against slavery and became the best-selling novel of its century.
dupotet-magie-devoilee-1852:
Dupotet unveils occult science in La Magie devoilee, in French from 1852, his flagship work. France's great magnetizer argues that the magnetic trance opens doors to hidden powers. Mesmerism and occult lore meet and merge across its confident, crowded chapters of doctrine and marvel.

He claims an ancient wisdom behind his modern practice of magnetism. Spirits, fluids, and secret traditions all find a place in his system. Later occultists cited the book across the rest of the century. It marks the bridge where the magnetic movement passed into the occult revival, a crossing that shaped French alternative science for decades.
kircher-oedipus-aegyptiacus-vol1-1652:
Athanasius Kircher attempts to read the hieroglyphs in Oedipus Aegyptiacus, Volume One, in Latin from 1652. Obelisks in Rome supply his texts, and Coptic his hoped-for key. Kircher got the details wrong, yet in trying he founded the serious study of ancient Egypt for the European world of his age.

Hundreds of engravings make the work a feast for the eye. Gods, rites, and symbols of Egypt fill its vast, learned pages. Jesuit missions fed his cabinet with reports from three continents here. The book stands as baroque scholarship at its most splendid, magnificent in scope even where its readings miss the mark entirely.
las-casas-brevisima-1552:
In 1552 Las Casas printed his Brevísima relación, a short account of ruin in the Indies. The Dominican friar addressed his sharp tract to the Spanish court itself. He meant to shock Spain into changing how it ruled the New World.

Page by page, he lists massacres, forced labor, and whole peoples wiped out. The style is brief, blunt, and built for outrage and action. Read at court and printed across Europe, the tract spread fast. It changed how Europe judged the Spanish conquest for good. Many still call it the most telling protest pamphlet ever written.
averroes-renan-averroes-et-laverroisme-1:
Ernest Renan published Averroes et l'averroisme in French in 1852, the first modern study of Averroes and his followers. Renan was a young French scholar when he wrote the book as his doctoral work. Averroes, the twelfth-century thinker of Cordoba, had been half forgotten in the West despite his fame as Aristotle's great commentator.

Renan traced how Averroes read Aristotle and how Latin followers turned his teaching into a bold doctrine of reason's independence from faith. He followed that influence through both Muslim and Christian schools. The book put a daring medieval mind back at the center of philosophy's history. It also launched Renan's career and set the pattern for later studies of how Greek thought passed through Arabic hands into Europe.
cia-0000008652:
Quang Yen district, in Quang Ninh province, is named in a June 1974 report on a dead American pilot sighted there. Quang Ninh borders China and holds Ha Long Bay's coast, far northeast of Hanoi. The sighting reached the files well after the 1973 ceasefire.

Reports from remote districts tested the reach of the postwar accounting system. A witness account had to travel far before analysts could match it to a loss. Many never matched, yet all were kept. Keeping them mattered because later evidence sometimes completed an old fragment. This file is one such fragment, preserved with its place and date.
cia-0000010252:
A living American prisoner and the body of a helicopter crewman appear in the same January 1974 item, from a place the title cuts off. The pairing compresses the postwar search into one report: one man to keep seeking, one to bring home. Helicopter crews left many such paired cases.

Mixed reports forced two kinds of follow-up at once, hope and recovery. Analysts split the item and sent each half down a different channel. Both halves stayed linked by the shared incident. This file preserves the pairing as it arrived, a small emblem of the accounting's double duty in 1974.
cia-0000010552:
The situation in the Khe Sanh area, with refugees and the Laotian side of Khe Sanh named in its heading, fills a January 1968 spot report. Khe Sanh was a Marine combat base near the Laotian border, weeks from its famous siege. Spot reports carried fresh, local detail rather than finished analysis.

Refugees in the heading remind readers that civilians filled the ground armies fought over. The Laotian angle mattered because supply routes and sanctuaries crossed that border. A spot report's value is its nearness to the moment. This one preserves the Khe Sanh area as seen just before the siege began.
cia-0000013852: A CIA note dated June 3, 1967, reports an American prisoner held in NVN, the short code for North Vietnam. The title gives no name, camp, or town. Still, the place mattered: prisoners in the north entered a camp system run from Hanoi. Short notes like this helped map where captured men were being held.
cia-0000015352: A meeting of the OSI advisory group on UFOs fills a CIA file dated January 3, 1953. The meeting ran from January 14 through 17 that year. OSI was the agency's science office. Those four days match the famous panel that judged the saucer evidence and called for calm study. The meeting file of the OSI group is held in the CIA Reading Room.
cia-0000015452: Nothing But the Facts on UFOs, or Which Novosti Writer Do You Read, is the teasing title of a CIA item dated March 2, 1968. Two articles came with it, judging by the clipped title. The letter is a small, clear look at how orders moved from a war-time capital to a lone post in Japan.

On 30 October 1862, Christopher G. Memminger wrote to Stephen R. Mallory. Memminger ran the Confederate treasury; Mallory ran its navy office. The letter is document 52 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863, in the Confederate group printed there.

Letters between the South's money chief and its navy chief dealt with the cost of the sea war. Ships built abroad ate cash the treasury did not have. This one shows the two men at their desk work in Richmond, weighing bills against a shrinking purse. It is a home-office piece among letters to Europe, and it rounds out the group with the view from inside.
frus-1863p1-d152:
On 10 April 1863, Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to Charles Francis Adams, and a second letter to him bears the same date. Adams was the American minister in London. This letter is document 152 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

Seward's pairs that spring kept the London brief oiled as the ship fight turned. Each sheet took a head: a claim here, a word of tone there. This letter opens the pair of 10 April. It shows Washington working the file in its set rhythm. It ran ten days behind the news from London and ten days ahead of the talks to come.
frus-1863p1-d252:
To guide his minister in London, Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote these orders on 29 July 1863 to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. They stand as document 252 of the 1863 volume. The text is preserved in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume, which gathered the year's diplomatic mail for Congress and the public.

Orders crossed the Atlantic by steamship and took ten days or more to arrive. By the time Adams acted, events in London could already have moved on. Kept with the rest of the 1863 papers, it forms part of the fullest record of how the Union handled its most dangerous foreign relationship.
frus-1863p1-d352:
On 6 January 1863, Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington, sent this note to Secretary of State William H. Seward in Washington. It appears as document 352 of the 1863 diplomatic papers. The document comes from the Foreign Relations of the United States, the government's own published record of Civil War diplomacy.

The channel between Lyons and Seward was the main safety valve of Anglo-American relations in the war. Papers like this one are the valve at work. It dates from the month the Emancipation Proclamation took effect, which changed the politics of the war in Britain at once. Set in its place in the volume, it helps readers trace how two governments talked their way past repeated crises.
frus-1863p1-d452:
Lord Lyons, the British minister in Washington wrote this official letter to William H. Seward, Secretary of State on 8 April 1863. The two men at the ends of this channel, Seward in Washington and Lyons speaking for Britain, wrote to each other almost daily. It appears in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the State Department volume printed with the President's annual message for 1863.

Much of the mail between the two offices turned on ships: the Union blockade, seized cargoes, and Confederate agents buying vessels in British ports. For historians, the value lies in the run of the letters. Together they trace, almost day by day, how the Union kept its most dangerous foreign problem from boiling over. Readers who work through the file in order will find this letter where the clerks of 1863 left it, in the middle of the stream.
frus-1863p1-d552:
On 6 June 1863 a formal note passed from Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington to William H. Seward, the Secretary of State. The State Department later published the letter in its 1863 foreign affairs volume, laid before Congress with the President's message. The exchange belongs to the Civil War years, when Washington's first task abroad was keeping Europe out of the fight.

Letters like this one were the tools of a quiet contest. The Union meant to keep Britain out of the war, and it made that case note by note. Single letters rarely settle anything here. Their worth is in the chain they form, which lets a reader watch a dispute rise, cool, and fade in real time. Kept with the rest of the 1863 papers, it helps the full story of wartime diplomacy stay traceable, letter by letter.
frus-1863p1-d652:
Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London sent an official note to William H. Seward, Secretary of State on 30 October 1863. At the time, the Union government was fighting the Confederacy at home and working to keep foreign powers neutral. The letter was later printed in the 1863 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, issued with the President's annual message.

That autumn the sharpest issue was the pair of ironclad rams built for the Confederacy at Birkenhead. Britain held them back, and this mail ran while that fight played out. The real subject under all the polite wording was British neutrality. Washington wanted it kept strict, and London wanted no quarrel it could avoid. Alone it is one note among hundreds. In place, it is part of how a war stayed between the two sides that started it.
plos-pbio-0020152:
Paolo Norio and Carl L. Schildkraut studied how a virus copies its DNA in PLOS Biology in 2004. Epstein-Barr virus lives in human cells as small DNA rings called episomes. Each ring must be copied once per cell cycle, from start points that can shift.

The team found that where copying starts on the ring is flexible, a trait called plasticity of initiation. The virus does not depend on one fixed start site. That freedom may help it persist in many cell states without failing to copy. Epstein-Barr virus is tied to several cancers, so its copying rules matter. Knowing them can point to weak spots in how the virus maintains itself.
plos-pbio-0020352:
Jeb Gaudet, Srikanth Muttumu, Michael Horner, and their team charted gene activity in the early gut in PLOS Biology in 2004. The foregut gives rise to organs like the liver, lungs, and pancreas. Using the worm C. elegans, the team read gene activity across the whole genome as the foregut formed over time.

The time series shows waves of genes switching on in order, each wave preparing the next stage. Many of those genes match ones used in our own gut organs. A simple worm thus gives a timed script for a process that is hard to watch in mammals. The data set serves labs that study organ birth defects and stem cell work aimed at growing gut tissue.
plos-pone-0000152:
Raffaele Vardavas and Sally Blower published this modeling paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. It looks at Botswana, where HIV treatment programs had expanded, and asks when transmitted drug resistance would pass the World Health Organization's detection threshold. Transmitted resistance means new infections already carry virus that resists first-line drugs.

As treatment scales up, some resistance is expected to spread; the question is how fast. The authors model the rise of resistant virus in the population. Their timing estimate helps treatment programs plan surveillance, so resistance gets spotted by testing rather than by watching patients fail therapy.
plos-pone-0000252:
Guangcheng Zhang, Amir H. Assadi, Robert S. McNeil, and colleagues published this neurobiology paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. Reelin is a signal that guides young neurons to their places in the developing brain, acting through a receptor called VLDLR. The authors show that the Pafah1b complex, tied to the brain disorder lissencephaly, interacts with that receptor.

When brain layering goes wrong, as in lissencephaly, children face severe disability. Connecting Pafah1b to the Reelin pathway joins two lines of evidence about how layers form. The paper helps explain how migrating neurons read their directions during development.
plos-pone-0000352:
Roy R. Chaudhuri, Chuan-Peng Ren, Leah Desmond, and colleagues published this bacterial genomics paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. Genome sequencing of European isolates of Francisella tularensis subspecies tularensis, the tularemia bacterium, shows a surprise. They are almost identical to the US laboratory strain Schu S4, a strain kept in labs for decades.

Wild strains from Europe matching an old lab strain so closely is odd for a bacterium. It hints that this subspecies changes very slowly and spread only in recent times. Tularemia is a watched disease, so its family history matters when tracing outbreaks.
plos-pone-0000452:
Anthony I. Jack and colleagues charted how the brain's visual territory is organized, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. Vision begins in early visual cortex, at the back of the head, and spreads forward into extra-occipital regions that handle faces, places, and objects. The team studied changing human visual field organization along that route.

A visual field map records which part of what you see each patch of cortex handles. As maps change from early to later areas, they reveal how the brain trades precise geography for meaning. Understanding that organization underlies work on vision loss and on how the brain rebuilds the world from the eye's signals.
plos-pone-0000552:
Patrick S. Sullivan and colleagues studied why some HIV patients skip their medicine, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. Antiretroviral therapy works only if taken consistently; missed doses let the virus rebound and develop resistance. The team identified patient and regimen characteristics associated with self-reported nonadherence to therapy.

Knowing who struggles, and with which kinds of regimens, lets clinics target support instead of blame. Simplifying regimens and matching them to patients' lives are practical responses. Adherence research of this kind quietly determines whether powerful drugs deliver their trial results in the real world.
plos-pone-0000652:
Létitia Jean, Benjamin Thomas, Abdessamad Tahiri-Alaoui and colleagues revisited a suspect enzyme in Alzheimer's disease for PLOS ONE in 2007. Diseases of abnormal protein folding need an initial trigger, which may be infectious, inherited, inflammatory, or unknown. Cutting proteins into vulnerable pieces, such as the amyloid-beta peptide, can start the aggregation.

Their angle is heterologous amyloid seeding, one protein's aggregates seeding another's. They ask what role acetylcholinesterase, an enzyme long tied to Alzheimer's, plays in that seeding. The question revisits an old player with a new mechanism in mind. If one aggregate can seed others, the spread of damage in the brain reads differently.
plos-pone-0000752:
Andy Gardner, Stuart A. West and Ashleigh S. Griffin asked whether a survival trick in bacteria counts as social behavior. Antibiotic resistance by mutation is well reported. Less known are persister cells, which resist antibiotics not by inheritance but by switching to a slow-growing state that drugs cannot kill. Within one population, only some cells make that switch.

If persisters protect their relatives by outlasting treatment, persistence could be a social trait maintained for the group's sake. Their 2007 PLOS ONE paper tests that framing. The answer shapes how doctors think about relapsing infections, and how evolution explains cells that seem to sacrifice growth for the colony.
plos-pone-0000852:
Jianing Wei, Lizhong Wang, Junwei Zhu and colleagues showed that plants call in wasp bodyguards with a specific scent chemical, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Plant volatiles play an important role in defending plants against insect attacks by attracting their natural enemies. Green leaf volatiles and terpenoids emitted from herbivore-damaged plants were known to help parasitic wasps locate hosts, the caterpillars the wasps lay eggs in.

Their title narrows the signal: plants attract parasitic wasps by releasing hexenol, one green leaf volatile. A single named molecule makes the defense testable and usable. Farmers could one day spray hexenol-like signals to summon wasps instead of spraying insecticide.
plos-pone-0000952:
Wolfgang Forstmeier asked whether female birds differ in their own readiness to mate outside the pair, in a solo PLOS ONE article from 2007. Extra-pair paternity is common in wild birds, and many studies count how often it happens. Much less is known about whether individual females have a stable personal tendency toward it.

Forstmeier separates the female's own propensity from the push of circumstance. If readiness is a lasting trait, it could evolve like any other. If it is mostly situation, then opportunity rules. The question reframes a familiar field result: behind every extra-pair brood sits a female decision, and those decisions may not be equal.
plos-pone-0001052:
Ansar Pathan, Clare Sander, Helen Fletcher and colleagues tested boosting the TB vaccine with a modified virus, in PLOS ONE in 2007. BCG is the standing tuberculosis vaccine, and its protection fades. The booster candidate, MVA85A, is a modified vaccinia virus carrying a TB antigen called 85A.

The team investigated the safety and immune effects of giving the boost shortly after BCG. They compared results with BCG alone and with an earlier trial using a longer interval. Timing can make or break a booster, since the first vaccine's response is still rising. Their comparison helps set the schedule for larger efficacy trials.
plos-pone-0001152:
Some macaques infected with SIV, the monkey relative of HIV, keep the virus under tight control. John Loffredo and colleagues studied these elite controllers in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Killer T cells are widely accepted to play a key role in holding immunodeficiency viruses down.

The team showed that CD8 T cells from the controller monkeys recognize viral pieces presented by a molecule called Mamu-B*08. They also tracked how the virus varied under that immune pressure. Work like this parallels human studies of HIV control and informs what a vaccine would need to achieve.
plos-pone-0001252:
When yeast cells meet DNA-damaging agents, they switch on a massive program of gene activity. Ivan Rusyn and colleagues sorted out which part of that program answers DNA damage specifically, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. The complication is that damaging agents also harm other cell components, proteins and membranes included.

The authors studied transcriptional networks in Saccharomyces cerevisiae linked to an accumulation of intermediates from base excision repair, the pathway that fixes small DNA lesions. By tying gene responses to those repair intermediates, they isolate the DNA-specific signal. The work clarifies how cells sense and answer genome damage.
plos-pone-0001352:
Paramecium bursaria is a single-celled organism that carries several hundred green algae living inside itself. Toshiyuki Takahashi and colleagues studied its internal streaming, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. The cell shows rotational, microtubule-based cytoplasmic streaming. Granules and the symbiotic algae flow in a constant direction. Why the flow matters was unclear.

The authors report that arrest of cytoplasmic streaming makes the algae multiply in the green paramecia. Stop the flow, and the resident algae grow fast. That coupling suggests the host uses streaming to manage its tenants. It is a neat finding about how the two partners live together.
plos-pone-0001452:
Jo Fleming and co-authors published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on blood vessel loss in scleroderma. In this immune ill, harm to small vessels drives much of the disease burden. The team used stains and gene readouts to chart vessel state in patient tissue. They asked whether stem cell care can grow vessels back.

Their data explore whether treated patients show signs of new vessel growth. They also weigh whether the disease traits can in part reverse. Small vessel repair would be a real shift for a disease with few good options. The study gives a base for larger trials of stem cell care in scleroderma.
plos-pone-0001552:
Geoffroy Berthelot and colleagues published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on the arc of world records in sport. Records show the top edge of human speed and strength. The team charted how records have risen over time and what shaped that rise. Past gains had come in a near steady climb.

Their charts show the climb now bends toward a flat top. They read this as the close of a brief era of peak gains. Wars, drugs, gear, and wealth all left marks on the curve. A flat top would shift sport's focus from raw records to other forms of contest.
plos-pone-0001652:
Rulong Shen, Yin Ye, Li Chen, and their co-authors asked where the blood vessels inside tumors come from, in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Tumors need new vessels to grow, invade, and spread. Most accounts credit angiogenesis, in which nearby vessels sprout into the tumor. But tissue studies had hinted that tumor cells themselves might seed the vessel lining.

The team worked with precancerous stem cells, cells that are not yet full cancer but are on the way. Their results support the idea that such cells can act as progenitors for tumor vessels. The full text gives the cell markers, the vessel structures they formed, and the tumor tests. If tumors build part of their own blood supply, drugs that only block vessel sprouting may miss a route of growth.
plos-pone-0001752:
Usha Chinappen-Horsley, Glen M. Blake, Ignac Fogelman, and their co-authors hunted genes for bone length in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Human height is highly heritable but complex, and finding its genes had proven harder than expected. One reason may be that height lumps many bone lengths into one noisy measure.

Using DEXA imaging, which measures bones precisely, in the Twins UK cohort, the team ran a genome-wide linkage scan for bone lengths. They report quantitative trait loci on chromosome 5. The full text gives the twin data and the linkage peaks. Measuring single bones instead of total height is a cleaner way to find the genes that build the skeleton.
plos-pone-0001852:
Federica Chiara and co-authors studied a sugar burning enzyme's role in cancer cell death in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Type II hexokinase is made in excess in most tumor cells and mainly sits on the outer mitochondrial membrane. Its release from mitochondria triggers apoptosis, the cell's self-kill program. The standard model held that its contact with voltage-dependent anion channels kept cells alive.

The team reports that hexokinase II release triggers apoptosis through the permeability transition pore, without needing voltage-dependent anion channels. The full text gives the cell tests. Changing the model matters because drugs built to pry hexokinase off mitochondria are a live cancer plan.
plos-pone-0001952:
Jinhong Hu and co-authors ran a first human safety test of a malaria vaccine in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. The vaccine is built from a fused protein that joins parts of two proteins from the malaria parasite, AMA-1 and MSP-1. In rabbits and monkeys, the fused protein raised antibodies that block the parasite.

The phase one trial gave the vaccine, mixed in an oily carrier called Montanide ISA 720, to healthy adults. It was randomized, partly blinded, and used a dummy dose for comparison, with doses raised in steps. First trials like this check safety and immune response before any test of real protection.
plos-pone-0002052:
John Lin and co-authors mined six years of neuroscience meeting abstracts, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Annual meeting abstracts from scientific societies hold rich arrays of information about a field. The team extracted and processed abstracts presented at the Society for Neuroscience meetings from 2001 to 2006.

By computing over titles and text at scale, they aimed to distill the state and dynamics of neuroscience. They tracked what topics rose, which faded, and how the field's language shifted. Abstract mining of this kind turns a yearly flood of talks into a map a whole field can read about itself.
plos-pone-0002152:
Jae Myoung Suh, Drew Stenesen, John Peters, and co-authors hunted for genes that control lifespan in the fruit fly, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Fat-storing tissue has been shown to sway how long flies live. The team used a screen in the fly's fat body, inserting genetic switches to find genes that change longevity.

Their screen turned up a sorting nexin, a protein that helps route cargo inside cells, carrying a domain tied to signals that switch genes off. The find links the cell's internal sorting work to the pace of aging. Small steps like this build the case that lifespan is set by concrete, testable pathways.
plos-pone-0002252:
Iñigo Angulo-Barturen, María Belén Jiménez-Díaz, Teresa Mulet, and co-authors built a mouse model for the deadliest malaria parasite, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Plasmodium falciparum causes most malaria deaths, and new drugs and vaccines are urgently needed. Testing them was blocked by a simple fact: the parasite infects human red blood cells almost exclusively, so standard lab animals would not do.

The team engrafted mice with human red blood cells and selected parasite strains able to grow in them. The resulting model lets researchers test drugs against falciparum malaria in a living system. A reliable animal model speeds every step of antimalarial drug development.
plos-pone-0002352:
Igor Petrunia and co-authors checked a safety question in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Could a plant bacterium that entered mouse blood switch on genes in mouse organs? Agrobacterium tumefaciens is the main tool for moving genes into plants, and its host range can stretch to other organisms in the lab. Agrobacterium species have also been isolated from human bloodstream infections.

That raised a safety question: could bacteraemia, bacteria in the blood, lead the bacterium to deliver its genes into animal tissues? The team reports it did not lead to reporter gene expression in mouse organs. The negative result is reassuring for the medical safety of a workhorse of plant biotechnology.
plos-pone-0002452:
Led by Hunter, a team of researchers published its study in PLOS ONE in 2008. The author list runs from Melissa G. Hunter, Morgan McLemore, Daniel C. Link, and others. Its subject is divergent Pathways in COS-7 Cells Mediate Defective Internalization and Intracellular Routing of Truncated G-CSFR Forms in SCN/AML. Expression of truncated G-CSFR forms in patients with SCN/AML induces hyperproliferation and prolonged cell survival.

before, we showed that ligand internalization is delayed and degradation of truncated G-CSFR forms is defective in patients with SCN/AML. What the team did, and why they did it that way, forms the core of the piece. For science readers, it shows how a small, well framed question can add a firm piece of knowledge to a much larger field.
plos-pone-0002552:
Research by Silva and co-authors came out in PLOS ONE in 2008. The author list runs from Nathan Silva, William C. Smith, and others. Its subject is inverse Correlation of Population Similarity and Introduction Date for Invasive Ascidians. The genomes of many marine invertebrates, including the purple sea urchin and the solitary ascidians Ciona intestinalis and Ciona savignyi.

Analysis of the C. Each part of the study builds on the part before it, in the order the team carried it out. Readers finish with a clear sense of the problem, the approach, and why the question was worth the team's time.
plos-pone-0002652:
Work by Yujun Cui and colleagues appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was insight into microevolution of yersinia pestis by clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats. The full author list in the catalog record begins with Yujun Cui, and the article appeared in the open journal PLOS ONE.

The opening of the abstract sets out the basis for the work. Yersinia pestis , the pathogen of plague, has greatly influenced human history on a global scale. Anyone studying the topic can use the article to see how the authors framed the problem at the time of publication.
plos-pone-0002752:
Work by Berta Victoria and colleagues appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was conservation of the s10-spc-α locus within otherwise highly plastic genomes provides phylogenetic insight into the genus leptospira. The catalog record names Berta Victoria first among the authors, and the source is the open journal PLOS ONE.

The opening of the abstract sets out the basis for the work. S10-spc-α is a 17.5 kb cluster of 32 genes encoding ribosomal proteins. The authors add a further point. This locus has an unusual composition and organization in Leptospira interrogans . For readers, the value lies in how plainly the abstract sets out the problem and what the authors set out to test or describe.
plos-pone-0002852:
Work by Nikola Sprigg and colleagues appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was a randomised controlled trial of triple antiplatelet therapy (Aspirin, clopidogrel and dipyridamole) in the secondary prevention of stroke: safety, tolerability and feasibility. Authorship is credited in the record to Nikola Sprigg and co-authors, with PLOS ONE as the journal of publication.

The opening of the abstract sets out the basis for the work. Aspirin, dipyridamole and clopidogrel are effective in secondary vascular prevention. Its abstract frames the work for later readers, who can judge the full text against the aims stated at the start.
plos-pone-0002952:
Amanda Antons, Rui Wang, Spyros Kalams and co-authors measured how signal strength changes suppression by regulatory T cells in 2008. Regulatory T cells, or Tregs, calm immune responses to self and foreign targets alike. They need activation through their receptor and the signal IL-2 before they can suppress.

Writing in PLOS ONE, the team varied how strongly T cells were activated and watched Treg suppression of HIV-specific and general responses. Suppression depended on signal strength, as the title says. The detail matters for HIV, where both weak defense and excess activation cause harm. Full methods, data, and references appear in the complete article for readers who want more detail.
plos-pone-0003052:
Stephen Smith, David Tank, Lori-Ann Boulanger and co-authors argued in 2008 for stronger protection of endophytes. A key case for conserving biodiversity is that undiscovered species will yield products of great use to humans. That link was largely conjectural when the paper was written.

Endophytes are microbes living inside plants. Using direct bioassay evidence, the team supports the claim that such hidden life can yield bioactive compounds. Their title says bioactive endophytes warrant intensified exploration and conservation. Published in PLOS ONE, the paper ties drug discovery to habitat protection with data rather than hope.
plos-pone-0003152:
Ruud M. Buijs, Jan van der Vliet, Mari-Laure Garidou and colleagues trace how the brain talks to the spleen in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Vagus nerve output from the central nervous system had lately been shown to suppress the innate immune defence against pathogens. The team used anatomy and physiology methods to study brain-spleen communication directly.

The title gives the result: cutting the vagus supply to the spleen stopped the making of antibodies against antigens in the blood. Readers see hard evidence that nerves help set antibody output. The work links brain circuits to immune control in a concrete way.
plos-pone-0003252:
Torsten Thomas and co-authors read the genome of a sea bacterium in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. In the sea, germs crowd onto host surfaces like seaweed and shell-less animals, where they compete hard with each other. Pseudoalteromonas tunicata is a winner on such surfaces, known for holding its ground against rivals.

Their genome scan shows traits of a life lived stuck to surfaces in the sea. Readers see genes matched to that attached life style. Such traits, from glues to germ-killing tools, interest work on ship fouling and on new antibiotics.
plos-pone-0003352:
Helene A. Haeberle, Carin Dürrstein, Peter Rosenberger and colleagues study a hypoxia factor during viral infection in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Hypoxia-inducible factor 1 alpha is a transcription factor that functions as master regulator of mammalian oxygen homeostasis. Recent studies also identified a role for HIF-1 alpha as transcriptional regulator during inflammation or infection.

The title reports oxygen-independent stabilization of HIF-1 during RSV infection. Readers learn a respiratory virus can switch on an oxygen sensor without low oxygen. That crosstalk may worsen airway inflammation, and it suggests HIF blockers could be tested in severe viral infection.
plos-pone-0007452: Mycoplasma genitalium, one of the smallest known bacteria, carries a single nose-like structure called the terminal organelle that it must copy before dividing. This study shows two proteins, P110 and P140, hold that copying in check. The work reveals how even a minimal cell keeps its division machinery under tight control.
plos-pone-0007552: Cholera's watery diarrhea can drain the body so fast that the kidneys begin to fail. This study of patients documented the massive fluid volumes needed for treatment and flagged an unusual blood-chemistry ratio marking early kidney stress. The findings give clinicians concrete numbers for managing one of the world's most dehydrating infections.
plos-pone-0007652: Leeches can regrow muscle, and this study found the cells behind it: myoendothelial cells carrying both muscle and vessel markers. The researchers isolated and grew these dual-identity cells from leech tissue. The work offers a simple animal model for understanding muscle regeneration.
plos-pone-0007752: Glioblastoma is not one disease but several wearing the same name. This study sorted tumors into subclasses by which signaling pathways are active and which genomic alterations accompany them. The classification points each subtype toward its own treatment.
plos-pone-0007852: Blowflies are aerial acrobats, but most studies measure only their extremes. This study benchmarked the routine flight performance of Calliphora vicina in a novel mirrored arena. The normal envelope reveals what these insects actually do all day.
plos-pone-0007952: Party-drug euphoria got a serotonin dial. A 2009 PLOS ONE study by Doly's team pinned MDMA's reward on 5-HT2B receptors in mice. The drug flips serotonin transporters. The receptor dial was mapped. The dial feeds addiction science.
plos-pone-0008052: How muscles hold a steady grip was explained without the old textbook formula. A 2009 PLOS ONE study by Zot and colleagues modeled tension in striated muscle as a balance among multiple states rather than a single curve. Calcium sets off contraction by moving tropomyosin, the protein strand that blocks the muscle fibers' grip. The multi-state model fits both the binding data and the tension curve, giving a fuller picture of the muscle's molecular teamwork.
plos-pone-0008152: Lab-grown retina cells were tested as a fix for blindness. A 2009 PLOS ONE rat study by Carr's team put retinal pigment epithelium grown from human iPS cells into the eyes of rats losing their sight. iPS cells are adult cells rewound to a stem-cell state, able to become any cell type. The team checked whether the grafts survived and shielded the rats' own light-sensing cells. The protective effects move iPS-based grafts closer to treating human retinal disease.
plos-pone-0008252: Frog fathers' shares were tracked from egg to tadpole. A 2009 PLOS ONE study by Sherman's team followed paternity skew through development in Peron's tree frog. Sperm competition sets the shares at fertilization, but embryo deaths can reshuffle them. The persistent skew shows winners stay winners. The finding validates paternity as a proxy for fertilization success.
plos-pone-0008352: A gut spirochete's attack was watched in a dish. A 2009 PLOS ONE study by Naresh's team showed Brachyspira pilosicoli latches onto cultured gut cells and damages them. The slow-growing germ colonizes the large bowel. The cell-culture assault reveals its pathogenic moves. The model enables studying a neglected bug.
plos-pone-0008452: Flu's footprint in Bangladesh was mapped. A 2009 PLOS ONE study by Zaman's team ran hospital-based surveillance of flu among outpatients across Bangladesh in 2007 and 2008. Dhaka's poor had shown heavy flu; the national picture was missing. The surveillance filled the gap. The seasonality data guide vaccine timing.
plos-pone-0008552: Two clock genes got distinct job descriptions. A 2010 PLOS ONE study by Pendergast's team teased apart Period2 and Period3 roles in the mouse circadian system. The body clock's gears were blurry. Dish tests separated their duties. The split clarifies how mammals keep time. The dish tests reveal the clock's division of labor.
plos-pone-0008652: Threatened corals' family ties got mapped. A 2010 PLOS ONE study by Hemond and Vollmer measured genetic diversity and connectivity in Florida staghorn coral. White-band disease devastated the reefs. The genetic map guides restoration. The ties reveal which reefs can reseed others.
plos-pone-0008752: Cell docks' electric twitch got decoded. A 2010 PLOS ONE study by Zohar's team found voltage shifts move charge in GPCR docks, tuning signal grip. The twitch's grip effect was mapped. The decode refines dock science.
plos-pone-0008852: Artery-clogging immune cells got a flexibility check. A 2010 PLOS ONE study by Khallou-Laschet's team assessed macrophage plasticity in experimental atherosclerosis. The immune cells' shape-shifting was mapped. The check informs heart-disease therapy.
plos-pone-0008952: A sight-sound trick got a reaching test. A 2010 PLOS ONE study by Tremblay and Nguyen showed goal-directed reaching reduces sensitivity to an audio-visual illusion in real time. The sensory-integration shift was measured. The test informs neuroscience.
plos-pone-0009052: A Parkinson's protein got a sugar meltdown. A 2010 PLOS ONE study by Chen's team found sugar tags melt alpha-synuclein into toxic blobs fast. The tag-driven meltdown was mapped. The meltdown feeds Parkinson's science.
plos-pone-0009152: Blood stem cells got a Gab2-STAT5 boost. A 2010 PLOS ONE study by Li's team showed Gab2 promotes hematopoietic stem cell maintenance synergistically with STAT5. The adapter-protein teamwork was mapped. The boost informs stem-cell therapy.
plos-pone-0009252: Angry immune cells got a stromal-cell calming. A 2010 PLOS ONE study by Maggini's team showed mouse mesenchymal stromal cells turn activated macrophages regulatory-like. The immune-calming effect was mapped. The calming feeds cell therapy.
plos-pone-0009352: Wild behavior got a brain-gene shield test. A 2010 PLOS ONE study by Guo's team tested a brain-gene shield against wild behavior. The gene-behavior tie was logged. The test feeds behavior science. The shield worked in three cohorts.
